context: life-safety systems (ventilation & fire) dominate the fit-out over the civil lining

brief.intro: A tunnel project bores or cuts a passage through ground for road, rail or utility use, and while the civil lining — TBM-bored, mined, or cut-and-cover — is the enabling structure, it is the life-safety fit-out that dominates the schedule and the commissioning risk for road and rail tunnels: ventilation, fire detection and suppression, and the tunnel SCADA/management system. The excavation method sets the pace of the civil works — TBM advance rate, mined-tunnel round length, or cut-and-cover bay sequence — but once the lining is complete the real complexity begins: jet-fan or longitudinal ventilation, fire detection wired to a deluge or suppression cause-and-effect matrix, emergency lighting and egress, and a tunnel management SCADA system that ties it all together. A utility tunnel is much lighter — often just lighting, power and drainage — so the fit-out scope must be read against what the tunnel actually carries. Your schedule stands or falls on the excavation advance rate, protecting portal and cross-passage interfaces, and leaving real commissioning time for the ventilation/fire cause-and-effect testing that road and rail tunnels cannot open without.

scope.name: Site establishment & portal works
scope.desc: Launch/reception shafts and portal structures at each end of the drive.

scope.desc: TBM advance, mined tunnelling (drill & blast / NATM), or cut-and-cover construction.

scope.desc: Invert slab, drainage channel, and sump/pump chambers along the bore.

scope.name: Cross-passages & niches
scope.desc: Emergency cross-passages, cable/services niches and walkways.

scope.name: Ventilation
scope.desc: Jet fans or longitudinal/transverse ventilation system, ducts and dampers.

scope.name: Fire life-safety
scope.desc: Detection, deluge/suppression, and emergency lighting and egress signage.

scope.name: Electrical & lighting
scope.desc: Power distribution and normal & emergency lighting along the tunnel.

scope.name: Tunnel SCADA & management systems
scope.desc: CCTV, comms/radio coverage and an integrated tunnel management system (TMS).

scope.name: Drainage pumping
scope.desc: Sump pumps and rising mains to the outfall.

scope.name: Testing, commissioning & handover
scope.desc: Ventilation mode tests, fire cause-and-effect, SCADA integration and handover to the operator.

must_get_right: The excavation method sets the whole programme's pace — TBM advance rate, mined round length, or cut-and-cover bay cycle must be based on realistic productivity, not best-case.
Ventilation and fire life-safety are the real schedule risk for road/rail tunnels, not the lining — leave genuine time for cause-and-effect testing; regulators will not accept a token test.
Protect portal and cross-passage interfaces — they are where excavation, lining and the fit-out trades all compete for the same confined space.
A utility tunnel is a much lighter build than a road/rail tunnel — don't apply the same ventilation/fire commissioning weight where it doesn't belong.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Excavation advance is modelled as a rate-based (metres/day or rings/day) repeating activity so the true bored or mined progress rate drives the tunnel-length duration, not an assumed generic rate.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: TBM or mined excavation typically runs a 24/7 or extended-shift calendar once launched, since stopping mid-advance is disruptive and costly. Fit-out trades — ventilation, fire, electrical, SCADA — run a standard calendar behind the excavation face; commissioning runs an extended calendar to protect test windows, often requiring possession or closure periods for rail or traffic tunnels.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs portal/shaft → excavation & lining advance (the rate-controlling activity) → invert → cross-passages → ventilation & fire fit-out → electrical & SCADA → integrated ventilation/fire commissioning → handover. Excavation advance rate is almost always the single biggest driver of overall duration; fit-out and commissioning follow the face at a set distance and become critical once excavation completes.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Ground conditions match the geotechnical baseline report — a differing ground condition is the classic tunnelling risk, not a planning input; design and life-safety strategy (ventilation/fire concept) are frozen before fit-out starts; a single TBM/excavation crew with no unplanned face stoppages; possession/closure windows for commissioning are secured in advance for live-corridor tunnels.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Ongoing production matched to advance rate

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Portal and shaft laydown areas are confined and shared by excavation spoil-removal, segment/lining delivery and, later, fit-out material access — spoil haulage and segment logistics are usually the binding constraint on advance rate. Fit-out trades work in a long, narrow, single-access corridor, so their sequencing along the tunnel length matters as much as the trade content itself.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: differing ground conditions slowing excavation advance, fit-out congestion in the confined tunnel bore, and a failed ventilation/fire cause-and-effect test forcing a re-test before regulatory sign-off. Schedule contingency is held on the excavation advance rate itself — a rate assumption, not a lump sum — and again before the integrated commissioning test.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client, by tunnel drive/section; controlled at Level 3, with excavation advance tracked as a rate-based repeating activity; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
